balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Beach Energy Limited: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Beach Energy Limited: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Beach Energy Limited: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Beach Energy Limited: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Beach Energy Limited: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Beach Energy Limited: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Beach Energy Limited: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Beach Energy Limited: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

reserves2p.title: 2P reserves and contingent resources
reserves2p.content:
2P reserves (proved + probable) are the volumes Beach's independent reserve certifiers judge more likely than not to be commercially recoverable from existing developments. 2C contingent resources are volumes that are technically recoverable but not yet committed for development -- Otway nearshore and Taroom Trough sit here, not in 2P.

For Beach Energy Limited: 2P reserves fell from 283 MMboe (FY2022) to 156 MMboe (FY2026) -- nearly halved in four years -- despite positive revisions from Western Flank drilling. This is the single biggest driver of the DCF's bear case: a producer that cannot replace what it extracts is running down a fixed asset, not compounding one.

What to watch:

  • Whether annual reserve bookings (additions + revisions) exceed the year's production
  • 2C-to-2P conversion via FID on Otway nearshore and Taroom Trough
  • Reserve write-downs following price or Cooper Basin/Waitsia performance disappointments

reserveLife.title: Production and reserve life
reserveLife.content:
Annual production is the MMboe actually extracted and sold in the year. Reserve life is 2P reserves divided by that year's production -- a rough-cut estimate of how many years the current reserve base lasts at the current extraction rate, ignoring future additions or decline curves.

For Beach Energy Limited: production has held roughly flat (18-19 MMboe/yr since FY2023) while 2P reserves kept falling, which is exactly why reserve life compressed from 13.2 years (FY2021) to 8.0 years (FY2026). Flat production concealed the reserve depletion until the ratio made it explicit -- the DCF's depleting-reserve model uses this reserve life, not trailing production growth, to shape the post-FY2029 decline path.

What to watch:

  • Reserve life continuing to compress even if production stays flat
  • FY27 production guidance (19.5-23.0 MMboe) versus actual, given Waitsia ramp-up risk
  • Any acceleration in production once reserve life falls below ~5-6 years, often a sign operators are producing out a field ahead of decline

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Beach Energy Limited: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Beach Energy Limited: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
